If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint AT the specified altitude, or AT OR ABOVE the specified altitude, the aircraft holds the specified altitude until arrival at the waypoint in FLC or PTCH descent mode. The aircraft keeps high altitude as long as possible and then descends to the waypoint constraint altitude in VPATH or VGP mode. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint BETWEEN two altitudes, the lower altitude is held. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint AT OR BELOW the specified altitude, no altitude will be held. VNAV honors only descent constraints. If the preselect altitude is lowered when the aircraft is in a constraint altitude, and an altitude change mode is selected, VNAV allows the aircraft to leave the constraint altitude. But, if the constraint is an AT, AT OR ABOVE or BETWEEN altitude, the message CHECK FPLN ALT shows on the CDU. This message also shows the selected VNAV when the aircraft is already below the next descent constraint altitude. When the aircraft is within the capture distance of a constraint altitude, the VNAV mode automatically switches to altitude hold, and remains in altitude hold until the descent is resumed.

The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) is activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). After ALT Mode is activated, if no other vertical mode (FLC or VS Mode) has been selected, the aircraft will continue to climb/descend due to inertia, and then descend/climb again to capture the baro pressure altitude when ALT Mode is activated. The VNAV Mode is deselected when the ALTV Mode is activated or when the FMS altitude is tracked in the ALTV Mode. If the APPR Mode is during GS capture, the ALT Mode will be inhibited.

The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust.

The primary flight control system is a fly-by-wire system where pilot control inputs are sent as signals to Actuator Control Electronics. These electronics combine the pilot's signals with sensitivity signals from the Flight Control Cabinet (FCC). The FCC calculates these sensitivity signals and augmentation commands based on aircraft sensor data to adjust the pilot's commands and then sends command signals to actuator servos to move the control surfaces.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is always armed except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. It arms during GA Mode if the preselected altitude is 75 ft greater than the current altitude. In contrast, the Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode is activated manually by pressing the ALT button, or automatically when the preselected altitude changes during ALTS Mode or ALTS Mode capture. When ALT Mode is activated, the aircraft will continue to climb/descend due to inertia before capturing the barometric pressure altitude if no other vertical mode is selected.

The system generates pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated when aircraft airspeed is less than Vman - 5 kt or Mach is less than Mman - 0.01, unless ALTS mode is captured or ALT mode is active. It provides pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. The USPD Mode exits automatically when the current airspeed/Mach is greater than Vman/Mman, and the airspeed reference is set to Vman + 5 kt/Mman +0.01, with the FG vertical Mode switching to FLC Mode. In USPD Mode, the SPEED Knob is inhibited, and most other vertical modes are inhibited unless in ALTS, ALT, TO, or GA Mode. The AT is armed in USPD Mode.

In this mode, the Autoflight System provides optimal escape maneuver commands by integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until the windshear warnings cease. If the constraint requires crossing at a specified altitude or at or below it, that altitude is held. For constraints between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is at or above a specified altitude, no altitude is held. If the preselect altitude is not raised to the flight plan target altitude or above, the preselected altitude is captured, sequencing the mode to VALTS, and VNAV will not sequence to climb VFLC until a climb mode selection is made.

The Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) is activated manually by pressing the ALT Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). The primary flight control system is a fly-by-wire system. The pilot sends control signals to the Actuator Control Electronics through cockpit control inputs. The Windshear Escape Mode (WS) is automatically entered when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. It provides optimal escape maneuver commands integrating airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data until windshear warnings cease. To manually exit, another vertical mode must be selected. In WS Mode, AT is set to TOGA thrust, and the autopilot disengages automatically after 2 seconds.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is activated when aircraft Mach number is more than Mmo + 0.01, or airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. It generates pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. The Go-around (GA) Mode is activated by pressing the TOGA Pushbutton. In this mode, pitch angle is commanded in accordance with the go-around target speed, with an initial lower limit pitch angle of 8° which reduces to 4°. The pitch command upper limit of the Flight Director expands to 30°, but the autopilot's pitch control upper limit remains at 20°. The target speed is the greater of VAPP or current speed, ranging from VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 20 kt during two-engine operation, and VREF + 5 kt to VREF + 15 kt during single-engine operation. In the roll axis, the commands hold the heading reference, with the bank angle limited to ±5°.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to AUTO. The INCR/DECRT Switch is used to set the required refuel quantity. Refueling starts when the Refuel Shutoff Valve is manually opened. The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the process and automatically closes the Refuel Shutoff Valve when the preselected quantity is reached. The FQC automatically records and displays the last preselected refuel quantity. To activate the FQC for automatic refueling, the INCR/DECRT Switch must still be operated even if the required quantity matches the displayed one. Automatic refueling balances fuel quantities between the left and right tanks. If an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb) occurs, the tank with the higher quantity is shut off. When balanced, both tanks are refueled. Refueling is completed when the combined total equals the preselected value.

The AUTOBRAKE Selector is used to select the required deceleration rate and has two operating modes: landing mode and takeoff mode. For takeoff, it can be set to RTO to arm the autobrake takeoff mode. For landing, it can be set to LO, MED, or HI to select a low, medium, or high deceleration rate respectively. It can also be set to OFF to disarm the autobrake.

The autobrake is disarmed after arming in any of the following conditions: The brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals disagree.
The Underspeed Protection Mode is inhibited in the following conditions: Radio Altitude is below 1000 ft; After GS mode is captured.
Braking starts automatically at the selected deceleration rate when the autobrake is activated, both thrust levers are at IDLE or in the reverser position, and these conditions have been met for 3 s.

The autobrake will disarm during application in any of the following conditions: The wheel brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO. The application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available and lasts for 1 s. One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight. Any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE.

The main functions of TCAS are to detect aircraft in its vicinity, display potential and predicted collision targets, and issue vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflict.

The ATC transponder replies to interrogations from ground stations for effective air traffic control. Mode S allows ground stations to have one-to-one interrogation and reply communications and has data link capability for coordination of anti-collision maneuvers. ADS-B OUT capability allows the ATC transponder to automatically and continuously transmit surveillance data to the ATC ground station.
The TCAS detection capability is limited to intruders flying within a maximum lateral range of 30 NM ～ 40 NM and within a maximum altitude range of 9900 ft (9900 ft above/below the aircraft).
The TCAS system can indicate up to 40 intruder aircraft simultaneously on the display.
One TCAS receiver/transmitter, Two TCAS directional antennas.

TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders. Depending on the replies, TCAS determines for each intruder its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude (using ATC mode C or S). Then, TCAS computes the intruder's trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA.
Its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude.
Its trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA.
When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered.
TCAS classifies intruders into Proximate traffic, Traffic Advisory (TA), and Resolution Advisory (RA). Other Traffic is also a classification for non-threat traffic.

Proximate traffic is identified as having no immediate collision threat, being in adjacent airspace within 6 NM laterally and ±1200 ft vertically. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as an unfilled cyan diamond.
Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when conditions change. The TAU for a TA is about 40 seconds.
TA is displayed on the PFD/ND as a yellow hollow circle. It provides aural alerts: "TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC".
Resolution Advisory (RA) signifies a real collision threat with a TAU of about 25 seconds.

Resolution Advisories (RAs) are displayed on the PFD/ND as a red hollow diamond and provide aural alerts such as "CLIMB, CLIMB", "DESCEND, DESCEND", "INCREASE CLIMB", "INCREASE DESCENT", "MAINTAIN VERTICAL SPEED", "LEVEL OFF".
The two types of vertical orders for an RA are "CLIMB, CLIMB" and "DESCEND, DESCEND".
Other Traffic refers to non-proximate traffic within the surveillance envelope that does not pose a collision threat. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as an unfilled cyan diamond.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to AUTO. The INCR/DECRT Switch is used to set the required refuel quantity. The Refuel Shutoff Valve is manually selected open to start refueling. The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the refueling process and automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when fuel in the tank reaches the preselected quantity. The FQC automatically records the last preselected refuel quantity. To activate the FQC for automatic refueling, the INCR/DECRT Switch must be operated even if the required quantity is the same as displayed. This mode ensures fuel quantities are balanced between left and right tanks.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, the FQC uses the following methods to ensure fuel balance: if an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb) exists, the tank with the higher quantity will be shut off. When the tanks are balanced, both tanks will be refueled. If the fuel imbalance between the two fuel tanks reaches 400 kg (882 lb) during refueling, the FQC will close the refuel shutoff valve in the tank with the higher quantity. When the fuel quantity is balanced, both refuel shutoff valves are opened to complete the refueling process simultaneously.

In manual refueling mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to MANUAL. Refueling personnel can open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch on the Refuel/defuel Control Panel.

The main components of the air conditioning process include: PACKs (to adjust temperature and pressure), mixing manifold (to combine air from PACKs and recirculation fans), trim air system (to add hot air for temperature control), and recirculation fans (to filter and move cabin air).

Bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted by two flow control valves and two PACKs for temperature and pressure. It then enters a mixing manifold to be combined with recirculated cabin air. Hot trim air is added in the air conditioning distribution duct before being sent to the cockpit and cabin.

The Flight Control Cabinets (FCCs) control the sensitivity for elevators, ailerons, and rudder, and the Spoiler Actuator Control Electronics (S-ACE) integrated within the FCCs control ground and multi-function spoilers. The Primary Actuator Control Electronics (P-ACE) receive pilot inputs and FCC sensitivity signals to drive elevators, ailerons, and rudder via Power Control Units (PCUs). The Horizontal Stabilizer Actuator Control Electronics (HS-ACE) receive stabilizer trim switch inputs and FCC sensitivity signals to drive the Horizontal Stabilizer Trim Actuator (HSTA).

In Normal Mode, the primary flight control system uses airspeed for sensitivity scaling and limiting. The sensitivity scaling of the rudder depends on airspeed, engine fault status, flap position, and aircraft on the ground or in flight status. Sensitivity scaling of the elevator depends on airspeed and flap position. Sensitivity scaling of the aileron and multi-function spoiler depends on airspeed. The Bob Weight function increases control column pitch feel during high "G" loads, and the Flight Control Cabinet (FCC) can decrease force fight through an alleviation algorithm. The FCC also compensates for configuration changes by adjusting stabilizer position and integrates speedbrake and roll assist commands. Ground lift dump automatically extends spoilers during landing or rejected takeoff to decrease lift and increase weight on wheels. Pitch trim rate is adjusted based on airspeed.

The transponder uses altitude data from the onside Air Data Computer (ADC), or cross-side if the onside is invalid or deselected.

The wing anti-ice valve controls the hot air flow of the wing anti-ice system.
The flow control valve is pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled.

The corresponding wing anti-ice valve closes automatically in any of the following conditions: Loss of electric power. Upstream pressure drops below 11.6 psi. When ANTI-ICE AIR SOURCE Selector is set to the opposite side.

The Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs) release pressure through the wing anti-ice valve when pressure builds up in the downstream high pressure line of the Pressure Regulating and Shutoff Valve (PRSOV) and any of the following conditions are met: Override either side of thrust lever more than 40°, Both flow control valves are closed, Both wing anti-ice valves are closed, Both ENG BLEED AIR Switches are shut off, Both Pressure Regulating and Shutoff Valves (PRSOVs) are closed, Not in the maximum takeoff (APR) thrust, Not in the one-side engine start status.

The pilot can manually select the engine bleed air source using the L (R) ENG BLEED AIR Switch on the BLEED AIR Control Panel. With the switch set to AUTO (light out), the engine bleed air system is automatically controlled by the Integrated Air System Controller (IASC). When the switch is OFF (white), the engine bleed air is shut off.
